title: Big Footprints Point to a Giant Mammal in Dinosaur Times
summary:
Picture a moonlit night, about 130 million years ago, in what is now southern Brazil. A large mammal walks across wet sand dunes, leaving tracks five inches wide.

Quarry workers found those fossil footprints in 2019. Scientists still do not know which animal made them. But the prints are nearly twice as big as the next-biggest mammal tracks from the same place. The animal walked on all fours, with short legs and paws, and was about the size of a cougar.

The find goes against an old idea. Since the 1800s, many scientists thought mammals stayed small while dinosaurs ruled. But other clues show some early mammals grew large. In Poland, bones of Lisowicia, a pig-like plant-eater as big as an elephant from about 205 million years ago, show an animal over eight feet tall and heavier than five tons.

Most mammals in dinosaur times were still small, often smaller than a house cat. But the fossil record is not complete, and more big mammals may be waiting to be found.
why_it_matters: It shows that what scientists believe can change when new clues turn up, just like when you find a new clue that changes your answer to a puzzle.

background_read: Long ago, dinosaurs lived alongside early mammals, which were mostly small animals with fur that fed their babies milk.
When an animal walked on soft ground, its tracks could harden into rock and last as fossils, so scientists can study them to learn how big the animal was and how it moved.
Finding very large tracks can change what scientists think about how big early mammals could grow.
